pos: n. pl. (the joints between leg and foot)
etymology: From the Saxon ancleow. The word stands once in the KJV text proper, and it marks the first of four measurements in Ezekiel's vision of the river that runs from the temple.
biblical_def: A man with a measuring line leads the prophet into a river, and the depth is recorded at each thousand cubits: “And when the man that had the line in his hand went forth eastward, he measured a thousand cubits, and he brought me through the waters; the waters were to the ankles” (Ezekiel 47:3). The ankles are the shallow end, and they are the point. The river does not begin as a torrent; it begins as water a man can wade without effort, and it grows by measured stages: “Again he measured a thousand, and brought me through the waters; the waters were to the knees. Again he measured a thousand, and brought me through; the waters were to the loins” (Ezekiel 47:4). At the fourth thousand the wading stops: “Afterward he measured a thousand; and it was a river that I could not pass over: for the waters were risen, waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over” (Ezekiel 47:5). The river is not fed by tributaries; it issues from the sanctuary and deepens on its own, and what it touches lives: “And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither: for they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh” (Ezekiel 47:9). The measurement at the ankles is where a reader stands at the beginning.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ankle as the joint which connects the foot with the leg.
webster_full: ANKLE, n. [Sax. ancleow.] The joint which connects the foot with the leg.
FORD, v.t. To pass a river or other water by treading or walking on the bottom.
RIVER, n. A large stream of water flowing in a channel on land toward the ocean, a lake or another river.
SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; the most retired part of the temple, where the ark was kept.
HEAL, v.t. To cure of a disease or wound and restore to soundness; to reconcile, as a breach.
scriptures: Ezekiel 47:3
And when the man that had the line in his hand went forth eastward, he measured a thousand cubits, and he brought me through the waters; the waters were to the ankles.
Ezekiel 47:4
Again he measured a thousand, and brought me through the waters; the waters were to the knees. Again he measured a thousand, and brought me through; the waters were to the loins.
Ezekiel 47:5
Afterward he measured a thousand; and it was a river that I could not pass over: for the waters were risen, waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over.
Ezekiel 47:9

And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither: for they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh.
corruption_summary: The rising river is turned into a metaphor for the believer's deepening spiritual experience, which relocates the source of the water from the sanctuary to the self.
corruption_paragraphs: The most common devotional use of Ezekiel 47 makes the four depths four stages of Christian maturity: ankle-deep believers who want more, and the challenge to go out further until one is swimming. The exhortation may be well meant, but it inverts the vision. Ezekiel is not choosing his depth; a man with a line is measuring and leading him, and the water is rising because of what it flows from, not because of the prophet's appetite. The river issues from under the threshold of the house. Its increase is a property of its source. Reading it as a chart of personal zeal quietly moves the miracle from the sanctuary into the worshipper.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the direction of the flow. Everything in the chapter moves outward and downward from the temple to the desert and to the Dead Sea, and what is healed is healed because the water arrived, not because it deserved water. The waters go into the sea and the sea is healed. That is the gospel's own shape, and it is why the New Testament closes with a river proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb. The believer's part in Ezekiel 47 is to be led in and to be one of the living things the river reached.

Hebrew berek (H1290) — the knees; the second thousand cubits.
Hebrew mothen (H4975) — the loins; the third measure before the water becomes impassable.
Hebrew nachal (H5158) — a torrent, stream; the river issuing from the sanctuary.
Hebrew raphah (H7495) — to heal, mend; the waters shall be healed.

“A river that I could not pass over” — the fourth thousand cubits.
“Every thing shall live whither the river cometh” — the effect of the water.

pos: n. pl. (the grinding teeth; the molars)
etymology: From grind, Saxon grindan. The Preacher uses the word of the teeth, in the allegory of old age that closes Ecclesiastes — a house whose servants are failing one by one.
biblical_def: Ecclesiastes closes with a portrait of a body described as a great house falling into disrepair: “In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened” (Ecclesiastes 12:3). The keepers that tremble are the hands, the strong men that bow are the legs, the grinders are the teeth, and the darkened windows are the eyes. The Preacher is not being coy; he is being merciful, giving a young man a picture he can carry before he needs it. The charge that governs the whole passage stands at its head: “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them” (Ecclesiastes 12:1). The decline ends where every man's does: “Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets” (Ecclesiastes 12:5). And then the verdict that sets the whole book upright: “Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7). Few teeth are a small thing. They are also a notice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grinder as one that grinds; and the grinders, the double teeth which serve to grind the food.
webster_full: GRINDER, n. One that grinds, or makes smooth by grinding; a grinding tooth; a double tooth; a molar.
GRIND, v.t. [Sax. grindan.] To break and reduce to fine particles or powder by friction.
TOOTH, n. A bony substance growing out of the jaws, and serving as the instrument of mastication.
DECAY, v.i. To pass gradually from a sound, prosperous or perfect state, to a less perfect state; to fail.
ALLEGORY, n. A figurative sentence or discourse, in which the principal subject is described by another subject resembling it.
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 12:3
In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened,
Ecclesiastes 12:1
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
Ecclesiastes 12:5

Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets:
Ecclesiastes 12:7
Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
corruption_summary: Ageing is reframed as a problem to be managed or defeated, and Ecclesiastes 12 is read as pessimism rather than as the kindest chapter in the book.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture that markets the reversal of age cannot read Ecclesiastes 12 without flinching, and so it does not read it. The chapter is filed under the Preacher's gloom and the reader moves on. But the passage is not lamenting decline; it is timing an appeal. Every image — the trembling hands, the bowed legs, the few grinders, the darkened windows — exists to give urgency to the imperative in verse 1, which is to remember the Creator while there is still strength to remember Him with. The honesty about the body is the mercy in the text, not the sorrow in it.

The second misreading is churchly sentimentality about the elderly, which honours age in the abstract while avoiding what Ecclesiastes says about it plainly: desire fails, fears come, and man goes to his long home. Scripture never pretends otherwise, and it never leaves the picture there. Dust returns to the earth and the spirit returns unto God who gave it — which means the decay of the house is not the end of the tenant, and that the One to be remembered in youth is the One to be met at the last. The doctrine is resurrection, and it is the only ground on which a man can look at his own failing grinders without despair.

pos: v. (to pierce; to make a hole through)
etymology: From the Saxon borian, to pierce. In the law it names the act that marked a servant who refused his freedom; in Job it names what no man can do to leviathan.
biblical_def: The word carries a statute that turns on love. A Hebrew servant completing his six years may go free, and if he will not, the refusal is made permanent in his flesh: “Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever” (Exodus 21:6). The reason he stays is stated in the preceding verse, and it is the only reason the law will accept: “And if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free” (Exodus 21:5). The ear is bored at the door of the house he has chosen. The second use is the LORD's challenge concerning leviathan: “Canst thou put an hook into his nose? or bore his jaw through with a thorn?” (Job 41:2). What a master may do to a willing servant, no man can do to that beast. Between the statute and the challenge lies the sentence the Psalmist speaks and the epistle to the Hebrews applies to Christ: “Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required” (Psalm 40:6). The willing servant with the bored ear is the Old Testament picture of the Son who said, Lo, I come to do thy will.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bore as to perforate or penetrate a solid body and make a round hole.
webster_full: BORE, v.t. [Sax. borian.] To perforate or penetrate a solid body and make a round hole.
AUL, n. A pointed instrument for piercing small holes in leather.
SERVANT, n. A person, male or female, that attends another for the purpose of performing menial offices for him.
MANUMISSION, n. The act of liberating a slave from bondage and giving him freedom.
DOOR-POST, n. The post of a door; the piece of timber on each side of a doorway.
scriptures: Exodus 21:6
Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever.
Exodus 21:5
And if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free:
Job 41:2
Canst thou put an hook into his nose? or bore his jaw through with a thorn?
Psalm 40:6
Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required.
corruption_summary: The statute is cited as evidence that Scripture endorses chattel slavery, which ignores both the six-year release it commands and the servant's own stated love as the sole ground for staying.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 21 is regularly produced as proof that the Bible institutionalises slavery, and the charge collapses on the text. The law before the reader is a manumission law: six years of service and the seventh year free, without payment. What the bored ear records is not a master's power to detain but a servant's refusal to leave — a refusal the law requires him to state aloud, in his own words, before judges, naming love of master, wife and children as his reason. A statute whose default is release and whose exception requires the servant's spoken love is not the institution its critics describe.

The corruption that matters more for the church is the loss of the type. The New Testament reads the willing bondservant as a picture of Christ, and Paul takes the title for himself — doulos, bondservant of Jesus Christ — as an honour rather than a humiliation. A church that flinches from the word loses the doctrine the word carries: that the Son freely took the form of a servant, that His obedience was not extracted but offered, and that those bought with His blood are not their own. The mark in the ear was made at a door. The believer's mark was made at a cross.

pos: adj. (fresh, not dried; of grapes, unripened into raisins)
etymology: From the Old French moiste, damp. In Scripture it occurs once, in the law of the Nazarite, where the separated man is cut off from the vine in every form it can take.
biblical_def: The law of separation is exhaustive about the vine: “He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink, and shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of strong drink, neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes, or dried” (Numbers 6:3). Moist grapes are fresh grapes; dried grapes are raisins; and between the two the statute has closed every door. The vow it belongs to is defined at the outset: “Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When either man or woman shall separate themselves to vow a vow of a Nazarite, to separate themselves unto the LORD” (Numbers 6:2). The thoroughness continues to the plant itself: “All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk” (Numbers 6:4). And the reason for the whole apparatus is given without embarrassment: “All the days of his separation he is holy unto the LORD” (Numbers 6:8). The law is not squeamish about grapes; Scripture elsewhere calls wine a gift that makes glad the heart of man. The point of forbidding a lawful good is that the abstaining itself is the sign. A Nazarite walking past a vineyard was a visible sentence about who owned his days.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines moist as moderately wet; damp; and applies it to fruit not dried.
webster_full: MOIST, a. Moderately wet; damp; as, a moist atmosphere or air.
NAZARITE, n. A Jew who professed extraordinary purity of life and devotion, and bound himself by a vow of separation.
SEPARATE, v.t. To disunite; to divide; to set apart for a particular purpose or use.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God; a solemn promise, by which a person binds himself to do or forbear something.
ABSTINENCE, n. In general, the act or practice of voluntarily refraining from the use of something.
scriptures: Numbers 6:3
He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink, and shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of strong drink, neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes, or dried.
Numbers 6:2
Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When either man or woman shall separate themselves to vow a vow of a Nazarite, to separate themselves unto the LORD:
Numbers 6:4
All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk.
Numbers 6:8
All the days of his separation he is holy unto the LORD.
corruption_summary: Voluntary abstinence is either dismissed as legalism or inflated into a mark of superior holiness, and the Nazarite's actual purpose — a visible sign of separation unto the LORD — is lost between the two errors.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite corruptions attach to this statute. The first, common wherever Christian liberty is prized more than it is understood, reads the Nazarite vow as the sort of scrupulosity the gospel abolished, and treats any voluntary abstaining as a return to bondage. The text does not support the caricature. The vow was temporary, voluntary, available to man or woman, and ended with a sacrifice and a haircut — the Nazarite went back to the vineyard. It was never a higher tier of Israelite; it was a season with a sign attached.

The opposite corruption is the older one, and the church has suffered more from it: abstinence treated as intrinsic merit, the abstainer as further along, the refusal of a lawful good as itself a virtue. Paul names this error directly when he writes of those forbidding to marry and commanding to abstain from meats which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving. The Nazarite gave up moist grapes and dried ones not because grapes are unclean but because separation needed a visible shape. Where the sign is mistaken for the holiness, the vow has become the thing the Reformers called will-worship.

“From the kernels even to the husk” — the thoroughness of the separation.
“He is holy unto the LORD” — the purpose of the whole statute.

etymology: A compound of fat + fleshed, formed to render the Hebrew phrase exactly. It occurs twice, both in Pharaoh's dream of the seven kine, and in both places it is paired with well favoured.
biblical_def: The dream that moved Joseph from a prison to a throne opens with cattle: “And, behold, there came up out of the river seven well favoured kine and fatfleshed; and they fed in a meadow” (Genesis 41:2). Pharaoh recounts it himself in the same words: “And, behold, there came up out of the river seven kine, fatfleshed and well favoured; and they fed in a meadow” (Genesis 41:18). What follows is the detail no one in Egypt could explain: “And the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke” (Genesis 41:4). The lean did not merely replace the fat; they consumed them and were no better for it, which is exactly how a seven-year famine consumes a seven-year surplus. Joseph refuses credit for the interpretation and gives the reason the dream came twice: “And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice; it is because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass” (Genesis 41:32). The fatfleshed kine are plenty, and plenty in Scripture is never self-explaining. It is a season God grants, with a term, and the wise man is the one who is told how long it lasts and believes it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fat as fleshy; plump; of full or plump habit of body, and kine as the plural of cow.
webster_full: FAT, a. Fleshy; plump; round; of full or plump habit of body; abounding with fat.
FLESHED, a. Fed with flesh; having flesh; used in composition, as fat-fleshed, lean-fleshed.
KINE, n. plu. of cow; cows; the old plural form retained in Scripture.
MEADOW, n. A tract of low land, appropriated to the culture of grass for hay.
FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country.
scriptures: Genesis 41:2
And, behold, there came up out of the river seven well favoured kine and fatfleshed ; and they fed in a meadow.
Genesis 41:18
And, behold, there came up out of the river seven kine, fatfleshed and well favoured; and they fed in a meadow:
Genesis 41:4
And the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke.
Genesis 41:32
And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice; it is because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass.
corruption_summary: The account is treated as a folk tale about a clever dream-reader, which removes the claim the chapter actually makes — that God established the thing and sent the warning.
corruption_paragraphs: Read as ancient literature, Genesis 41 is a court tale of the wise courtier who rises by his wits, a type found across the Near East. The chapter anticipates exactly that reading and refuses it in Joseph's first sentence to Pharaoh: it is not in me; God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace. Joseph claims no skill, gives no technique, and attributes both dream and interpretation to God. The doubling of the dream is likewise explained not as literary emphasis but as divine confirmation — the thing is established by God. To read the chapter as a tale of shrewdness is to delete the only explanation the text offers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the doctrine of seasons of plenty. Seven fat years were a gift and they were also a deadline, and the fat kine were eaten by the lean ones. Scripture's consistent counsel about abundance is that it is temporary, that it is given to be administered rather than consumed, and that the man who reads plenty as permanence is the fool of the parable whose barns were full the night his soul was required of him. Joseph's storehouses were an act of faith in a word from God about a famine no one could yet see.

pos: v. and adj. (throwing out foam; frothing)
etymology: From the Saxon fam, foam. Scripture gives the word twice: once of a boy convulsed by an unclean spirit, and once of false teachers likened to the surf of the sea.
biblical_def: Mark records what happened when the afflicted boy was brought to Christ: “And they brought him unto him: and when he saw him, straightway the spirit tare him; and he fell on the ground, and wallowed foaming” (Mark 9:20). The foam is the visible mark of a violence done to the child from within, and it appears the instant the boy is in the Lord's presence. The father's answer to Christ is the most honest sentence in the chapter: “And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief” (Mark 9:24). Jude uses the same image of men inside the church: “Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever” (Jude 1:13). The picture is precise. Surf throws up whatever the water is carrying, and what these men cast up is their own shame; the foam is not an accident of the storm but the content of the man. Isaiah had used the figure first: “But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt” (Isaiah 57:20). In both Testaments the foam is evidence — of a spirit that destroys, or of a heart that cannot be still.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines foam as froth; spume; the substance which is formed on the surface of liquors by fermentation or violent agitation.
webster_full: FOAM, n. Froth; spume; the substance which is formed on the surface of liquors by fermentation or violent agitation.
FOAMING, ppr. Frothing; throwing out foam; raging.
RAGE, n. Violent anger accompanied with furious words, gestures or agitation; fury.
SPUME, n. Froth; foam; scum; that which rises to the surface of liquor in violent agitation.
APOSTATE, n. One who has forsaken the church, sect or profession to which he before adhered.
scriptures: Mark 9:20
And they brought him unto him: and when he saw him, straightway the spirit tare him; and he fell on the ground, and wallowed foaming.
Mark 9:24
And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
Jude 1:13
Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.
Isaiah 57:20
But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt.
corruption_summary: The boy's affliction is reassigned wholesale to a purely medical category, and Jude's warning about teachers inside the church is softened into a comment about outsiders.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern handling of Mark 9 identifies the symptoms as epilepsy and concludes that the Gospel writers described in demonic terms what medicine now explains. Scripture does not permit the exchange. The narrative distinguishes plainly between diseases and possession, the Lord Jesus addresses the spirit directly and it answers, and He tells the disciples why their attempt failed. The dictionary affirms that God ordinarily governs the body by ordinary means and that illness is usually illness; it denies that the category of the unclean spirit can be dissolved into pathology because a modern reader finds it uncongenial.

Jude's foaming waves are not pagans. They are men who crept in unawares, who feast with the congregation, who are inside. That is the whole alarm of the epistle, and it is regularly blunted in the pulpit into a warning about the world outside the doors. The Reformed confessions keep the sharper edge: the visible church contains hypocrites, false teachers arise from among the flock, and the marks by which they are known are moral and doctrinal rather than social. What the surf casts up is what the water was carrying all along.

“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief” — the father's honest cry.
“Foaming out their own shame” — Jude on teachers within the church.

pos: n. pl. (restless turnings of a sleepless body)
etymology: From toss, of Northern origin, to throw or fling about. The word occurs once, in Job's account of his nights, and it is one of the most exact descriptions of insomnia in ancient literature.
biblical_def: Job is answering Eliphaz, and he answers with his nights: “When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day” (Job 7:4). The sentence has the shape of the thing it describes — lying down, calculating the hours, turning, waiting for a light that will not bring relief either. What he has been given instead of rest is stated just before: “So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me” (Job 7:3). The word appointed is not incidental; Job knows the nights were assigned, and he never pretends they arrived by accident. Then the speed of it: “My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope” (Job 7:6). David records the same experience in the Psalter without Job's bitterness but with no less weariness: “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6:6). Scripture does not hurry past these verses or apologize for them. A man of God may pass a night turning, counting hours, and finding the dawn no mercy, and the Bible writes it down.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines toss as to throw with the hand, and tossing as agitation; a throwing upward or from side to side.
webster_full: TOSS, v.t. To throw with the hand, particularly to throw with the palm of the hand upward; to throw or fling about.
TOSSING, n. The act of throwing upward, or from side to side; agitation; restlessness.
WEARISOME, a. Causing weariness; tiresome; tedious; fatiguing.
WATCH, n. A division of the night; the period of the night in which a person keeps awake.
AFFLICTION, n. The state of being afflicted; a state of pain, distress or grief; the cause of continued pain of body or mind.
scriptures: Job 7:4
When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day.
Job 7:3
So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me.
Job 7:6
My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope.
Psalm 6:6
I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears.
corruption_summary: Job's complaint is either sanitized into patience he did not display or reassigned to a clinical category that has no account of a night being appointed.
corruption_paragraphs: The proverbial patience of Job survives mostly because the book is not read past chapter two. From chapter three onward Job complains bitterly, accuses God of watching him too closely, and asks to be let alone that he may swallow his spittle. The habit of smoothing this away — quoting the blessing of chapter one and skipping to the restoration of chapter forty-two — robs the sufferer of the book's actual gift, which is that such speech is in the canon and that God, at the end, says Job spoke of Him the thing that was right.

The modern alternative is to hand the whole experience to clinical description and stop there. Sleeplessness is real and may have causes that ordinary means address, and Scripture nowhere forbids a man to use them. But the therapeutic frame has no room for Job's central claim, which is that wearisome nights were appointed to him. That word is the doctrine of providence applied to the worst hours of a life, and it is what makes the complaint prayer rather than despair. Job is not describing a malfunction. He is arguing with the One who assigned the night, which is a thing only a believer does.

Hebrew manah (H4487) — to appoint, number out; wearisome nights are appointed to me.
Hebrew amal (H5999) — trouble, wearisome toil; the months of vanity.
Hebrew ereg (H708) — a weaver's shuttle; the speed of Job's days.

“Wearisome nights are appointed to me” — the hours assigned, not accidental.
“I water my couch with my tears” — the Psalter's parallel.

pos: v. (bound about with strips of cloth, as a newborn)
etymology: From the Saxon swethel, a swathing band. To swaddle a newborn was the ordinary first care given to a child — washed, salted, and bound — and Scripture uses its absence to describe abandonment.
biblical_def: Jeremiah uses the word of children raised and then lost: “Thou hast called as in a solemn day my terrors round about, so that in the day of the LORD'S anger none escaped nor remained: those that I have swaddled and brought up hath mine enemy consumed” (Lamentations 2:22). Ezekiel uses its absence as the picture of Israel's origin, a foundling given none of the ordinary kindnesses: “And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all” (Ezekiel 16:4). No one bound this child; no one wanted her. What follows is the whole gospel of that chapter in one sentence: “And when I passed by thee, and saw thee polluted in thine own blood, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live; yea, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live” (Ezekiel 16:6). The LORD gives what the parents withheld. And then, in the fulness of time, the ordinary care denied to Israel was given by a young mother to her firstborn in a stable: “And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn” (Luke 2:7). The bands that mark a child as belonging to someone were put on the Son of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines swaddle as to swathe; to bind, as an infant, with cloths or bands.
webster_full: SWADDLE, v.t. To swathe; to bind as with a bandage; to bind, as an infant, with cloths or bands.
SWADDLING-BAND, n. A band or cloth wrapped round an infant.
NATIVITY, n. Birth; the coming into life or the world; particularly, the birth of Christ.
FOUNDLING, n. A deserted or exposed infant; a child found without a parent or owner.
SUPPLE, v.t. To make soft and pliant; to render flexible.
scriptures: Lamentations 2:22
Thou hast called as in a solemn day my terrors round about, so that in the day of the LORD'S anger none escaped nor remained: those that I have swaddled and brought up hath mine enemy consumed.
Ezekiel 16:4
And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all.
Ezekiel 16:6
And when I passed by thee, and saw thee polluted in thine own blood, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live; yea, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live.
Luke 2:7
And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel 16 is avoided for its severity or read as merely a shocking metaphor, and the sovereign grace at its centre — a word spoken over a child nobody claimed — goes unpreached.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 16 is among the least-preached chapters in the prophets, and where it is handled it is usually handled as an extended shaming of Israel. The structure of the chapter says otherwise. It opens with a child abandoned at birth, unwashed, unsalted, unswaddled, lying in her own blood in an open field — that is, with a person who has done nothing and can do nothing — and the first thing that happens to her is a word: Live. Everything the chapter later says about her unfaithfulness presupposes that she was alive only because God spoke. To skip the chapter is to skip one of Scripture's clearest pictures of grace preceding every response.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of ordinary infant care as Scripture assumes it. Cutting the cord, washing, salting, binding — these were the acts by which a household said this child is ours, and their absence in Ezekiel is the measure of an abandonment. When Luke records that Mary wrapped her firstborn in swaddling clothes, he is recording that the Lord of glory was received the way any loved child was received in that country, in a place where there was no room for Him. The incarnation is not decorated in that verse. It is made ordinary, which is the scandal.

“Thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all” — Israel as a foundling.
“Wrapped him in swaddling clothes” — the ordinary care given to the Son.

pos: v. (made moist; watered, as bones with marrow)
etymology: From moisten, to make damp. The word occurs once, in Job's description of the man who dies in full strength — a body still well supplied, brought to the grave in the middle of its prosperity.
biblical_def: Job is refuting the comfortable doctrine of his friends, that the wicked visibly suffer and the righteous visibly prosper, and he does it by describing two deaths. The first: “One dieth in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet” (Job 21:23), and then the detail that makes it vivid, “His breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moistened with marrow” (Job 21:24). This man was never reduced. He was well-fed to the end and died in his sleep. Against him Job sets the other: “And another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and never eateth with pleasure” (Job 21:25). And then the levelling sentence: “They shall lie down alike in the dust, and the worms shall cover them” (Job 21:26). Job's argument is not that God is unjust; it is that his friends' scheme of visible retribution cannot be read off the surface of a life, because the grave takes the fat man and the bitter man together and tells the observer nothing. Marrow in Scripture is the sign of abundance — a feast of fat things full of marrow — and here it belongs to a man whose ease proves precisely nothing about his standing before God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines moisten as to make damp; to wet in a small degree; and marrow as a soft oleaginous substance contained in the cavities of animal bones.
webster_full: MOISTEN, v.t. To make damp; to wet in a small degree.
MARROW, n. A soft, oleaginous substance contained in the cavities of animal bones; the best or choicest part.
PROSPERITY, n. Advance or gain in anything good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise.
RETRIBUTION, n. Repayment; return accommodated to the action; reward or punishment.
GRAVE, n. A pit or excavation in the earth, for the reception of a dead body; a tomb.
scriptures: His breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moistened with marrow.
One dieth in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet.
And another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and never eateth with pleasure.
They shall lie down alike in the dust, and the worms shall cover them.
corruption_summary: The prosperity of the wicked is explained away by promising visible reversal in this life, which is precisely the doctrine Job is dismantling and the doctrine his friends were rebuked for holding.
corruption_paragraphs: The error Job attacks in chapter 21 is not extinct; it is a growth industry. The teaching that faithfulness produces health and wealth, and that hardship signals hidden sin or insufficient faith, is the position of Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar restated in modern idiom — and the LORD tells them at the end of the book that they have not spoken of Him the thing that is right. Job's observation stands: some wicked men live at ease, die quietly with their bones full of marrow, and are buried with honour. Any doctrine that must deny this is denying what Scripture plainly records.

The opposite error is to conclude from the same facts that God does not judge. Job does not go there and neither does the canon. Psalm 73 walks the identical road — envy at the prosperity of the wicked, the confession that it was too painful until the Psalmist went into the sanctuary of God, and then the end: surely thou didst set them in slippery places. The Reformed answer holds both halves. Providence is not a mechanism readable from outward circumstances, and the final assize is certain. A man whose bones are moistened with marrow may be the most pitiable man alive, and nothing visible will tell you so.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaqah (H8248), to water or moisten; moach (H4221), marrow; shalanan (H7946), at ease, quiet; aphar (H6083), dust.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaqah (H8248) — to give drink, water, moisten; Job 21:24.
Hebrew moach (H4221) — marrow; only here in the Hebrew Bible.
Hebrew shalanan (H7946) — wholly at ease, tranquil; the manner of that death.
Hebrew mar (H4751) — bitter; the soul of the second man.
Hebrew aphar (H6083) — dust; they shall lie down alike in it.
usage: “His bones are moistened with marrow” — the well-fed man at his death.
“Another dieth in the bitterness of his soul” — the other end of the same argument.
“They shall lie down alike in the dust” — what the grave reports.

pos: adj. (scabby; afflicted with a scaling disease of the skin)
etymology: From scurf, Saxon scurf, a scaly crust on the skin. In Leviticus it is one of the blemishes that barred a son of Aaron from offering, and one of the defects that barred an animal from the altar.
biblical_def: The word appears twice in the law, and the symmetry between the two places is the whole doctrine. First of the priest: “Or crookbackt, or a dwarf, or that hath a blemish in his eye, or be scurvy, or scabbed, or hath his stones broken” (Leviticus 21:20). Then of the offering: “Blind, or broken, or maimed, or having a wen, or scurvy, or scabbed, ye shall not offer these unto the LORD, nor make an offering by fire of them upon the altar unto the LORD” (Leviticus 22:22). The same defect disqualifies the man who brings and the beast he brings. The law is careful to add that the blemished priest is not cast out of his family or denied bread: “He shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy” (Leviticus 21:22). He eats; he does not offer. Nothing here is a comment on the man's worth, and the New Testament shows what the whole arrangement was picturing: “But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:19). A flawless victim was required, and Israel never once had a flawless priest. Both shortfalls are answered in one Person.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scurvy as scurfy; covered or affected by scurf or scabs; scabby; diseased with the scurvy.
webster_full: SCURVY, a. Scurfy; covered or affected by scurf or scabs; scabby; diseased with the scurvy.
SCURF, n. A dry scab or scale formed on the skin; the scaly matter of the skin.
BLEMISH, n. Any mark of deformity; any scar or defect that diminishes beauty or perfection.
WEN, n. An encysted swelling or tumor; a fleshy excrescence growing on the body.
OBLATION, n. Anything offered or presented in worship or sacred service; an offering; a sacrifice.
scriptures: Leviticus 21:20
Or crookbackt, or a dwarf, or that hath a blemish in his eye, or be scurvy, or scabbed, or hath his stones broken;
Leviticus 22:22
Blind, or broken, or maimed, or having a wen, or scurvy, or scabbed, ye shall not offer these unto the LORD, nor make an offering by fire of them upon the altar unto the LORD.
Leviticus 21:22
He shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy.
1 Peter 1:19
But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:
corruption_summary: The blemish laws are read as ancient prejudice against the disabled, which ignores the provision made for the blemished priest and the typology the whole arrangement served.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern charge against Leviticus 21 is that it excludes the disabled from ministry out of superstition about bodily perfection. The text answers the charge itself in a verse that is rarely quoted alongside the accusation: the blemished son of Aaron eats the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy. He keeps his priestly standing, his inheritance, his food and his family; he does not approach the altar or the veil. The restriction is on one act, and the same restriction falls on the animals. What is being protected is not the dignity of the able-bodied but the integrity of a picture.

That picture is the point. Every element of Israel's worship was a shadow of good things to come, and a shadow must keep its shape or it teaches falsely. An unblemished victim offered by an unblemished priest was the shape; and since no son of Aaron ever fully answered to it, the shadow stood for centuries as a promise unpaid. Hebrews draws the conclusion the law was built to force: such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners. To read the blemish laws as social prejudice is to miss that they were designed to leave Israel waiting.
roots_summary: Hebrew garab (H1618), a scab or itch; yallepheth (H3217), a scabbed condition; mum (H3971), a blemish; Greek amomos (G299), without blemish.
roots_lines: Hebrew garab (H1618) — scurvy, a scabbing disease of the skin; Leviticus 21:20 and 22:22.
Hebrew yallepheth (H3217) — scabbed, a running sore; paired with garab in both lists.
Hebrew mum (H3971) — a blemish, spot, defect; the governing word of the chapter.
Hebrew lechem (H3899) — bread; what the blemished priest still eats.
Greek amomos (G299) — without blemish; of Christ the Lamb, 1 Peter 1:19.
usage: “Or be scurvy, or scabbed” — among the blemishes barring a priest from the altar.
“Ye shall not offer these unto the LORD” — the same defect in the victim.
“A lamb without blemish and without spot” — what the law was waiting for.
